articles.title: Russia and Ukraine: Societies transformed by war | Brookings
articles.text:
Commentary
Russia and Ukraine: Societies transformed by war

Anna Colin Lebedev

Anna Colin Lebedev

Senior Lecturer and Researcher, Institute of Social Sciences of Politics
- Paris Nanterre University

July 22, 2026

Editor's note:
On June 5, the Center on the United States and Europe at Brookings hosted Anna Colin Lebedev for the 21st annual Raymond Aron Lecture. This is a lightly edited version of Colin Lebedev’s delivered remarks.

When reflecting on the intertwined yet divergent paths of Russia and Ukraine, I often recall the story of one of my interviewees, Slava. I first met Slava in 2015 in Kyiv for a research project on the Ukrainian veterans of the Soviet war in Afghanistan. Born in the industrial Donbas to a steelworker and an engineer who had met in Russia, he entered military school in Kyiv in 1981 and became an officer in the Soviet Special Forces. He was among the servicemen who witnessed the last columns of armored vehicles leave Afghanistan during the waning years of the USSR. Upon the collapse of the Soviet Union, as his unit was stationed in Uzbekistan, he left the army and returned to Ukraine.
In the chaotic environment of the 1990s, Slava was forced to ensure his family’s survival. He found a position with a company importing excavators from China. For a former elite officer, this represented a profound crisis and a complete loss of social status. Nevertheless, he persevered, earned enough to buy an apartment in the Kyiv suburbs, and gradually found new professional paths, eventually becoming a writer and musician. Since 2014, his native city of Alchevsk has been occupied by pro-Russian forces and was later annexed by Russia.
When asked about his self-identification, he confessed that despite having mixed Russian, Ukrainian, and Belarusian origins, he had long seen himself as Russian. However, he gradually realized how little he knew about the history of Ukraine—the country of his birth and the one he had chosen. He began reading extensively, reevaluating his family history—specifically their deportation to Siberia during the Soviet repressions. His sister, having relocated to Russia, did not share this perspective: “She is totally Russian,” Slava commented.
At the time of our initial 2015 interview, he wrote and sang exclusively in Russian; yet, when we reconnected a few years later, he had completely switched to Ukrainian. Since the onset of the war in the Donbas, Slava has volunteered extensively to support the Ukrainian armed forces, traveling frequently to the frontline to perform for the troops. “Alchevsk is a Ukrainian city,” he recently posted on social media regarding his native town, “and we will free it from occupation.”
Slava’s path accurately illustrates the complexity of Soviet and post-Soviet destinies in this part of Europe: mixed identities, entangled lives, a painful history, and moments of radical transformation. While striking, his evolution from a Soviet military officer to a Ukrainian songwriter is highly representative of broader shifts within the post-Soviet space.
Comparing Russia and Ukraine
Russia and Ukraine share a part—but only a part, a point to which I will return—of their past. This shared context has shaped societies that resemble one another in various respects. Prior to the armed conflict, a casual traveler to both countries would have observed clear similarities in architecture and lifestyles. These similarities were also institutional. Obliged to construct their legislative and institutional frameworks rapidly after independence, post-Soviet Russia and Ukraine followed parallel paths, blending Soviet legacies with adaptations to new conditions.
Military legislation provides an excellent illustration. While the Soviet system relied on a mass army model, both countries implemented a hybrid model following the collapse of the USSR, combining conscription with professional military personnel. Both retained the inherited conscription infrastructure and military institutions. An observer walking into an enlistment office in either Russia or Ukraine during the 1990s would have struggled to distinguish between the two institutions. Similar commonalities existed in areas like housing, health care, and education, alongside shared cultural references. This encompasses not just classical canonical figures like Alexander Pushkin, but more significantly, the fabric of everyday culture: nursery rhymes, pop music, iconic cinema, and television.
Nevertheless, when the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Russia and Ukraine were already two distinct societies. Fundamentally, Russia had functioned as the center of the USSR, whereas Ukraine was positioned at the periphery. Furthermore, Ukraine’s history was far more complex than Soviet historiography acknowledged. Finally, each post-Soviet country was shaped by distinct geographical features, unique natural and economic resources, and a differing geopolitical position.
The narrative of the Russian state under Vladimir Putin has consistently denied the sovereignty and the very existence of Ukraine as a distinct society. This was explicitly formulated in the Russian president’s 2021 essay, “On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians,” which argued that Ukraine was a puppet state and an artificial nation. Since the outbreak of the war, however, Ukrainian resistance has continuously demonstrated the opposite. Reflecting upon these commonalities does not mean endorsing the Kremlin’s reading of history or of the present. Analyzing shared legacies illuminates the divergences and specifically the divergent paths these two societies have taken since the dissolution of the Soviet Union, particularly since the outbreak of hostilities in 2014.
Conventional wisdom dictates that war is deeply transformative, altering social logic while forging new social statuses, practices, and relationships with the state. Of course, this holds true in many respects. There is nothing ordinary about living under shelling, taking up arms, or having a relatively mobilized society. However, the sociology of societies at war demonstrates that wartime behaviors are heavily anchored in peacetime social dynamics. Wartime transformations are deeply rooted in preexisting social experiences, history, and values.
Analysts frequently rely on familiar binary frameworks when comparing Russia and Ukraine: authoritarianism versus democracy, an aging inner circle around Putin versus a young Ukrainian leadership, aggression versus resistance, and repression versus mobilization. My analysis adopts a different perspective, exploring three key dimensions that shape the evolution of both societies: the importance of adaptation as a primary social skill; the relationship of citizens to the state; and evolving perceptions of self and the other.
1. The two faces of adaptability
The first dimension to consider is adaptability. Adapting to a hostile environment is something at which both Russian and Ukrainian social actors excel. Resilience and informal practices were established skills for Soviet citizens, developed amid chronic shortages, ideological pressure, and systemic inefficiencies. Soviet citizens were required to constantly navigate between ideological discourses and everyday realities.
This expertise became crucial following the dissolution of the Soviet Union. During the chaotic transition to a market economy and the disintegration of social policies, surviving in unpredictable conditions was imperative. Those who carried on—in both countries—demonstrated remarkable innovation: navigating criminalized economies, establishing businesses, learning to survive independently of the state, and circumventing state-imposed norms. Conversely, those who failed to adapt quickly grew nostalgic for the Soviet regime, which offered stable social policies and a sense of pride and belonging.
These skills sustained Russians and Ukrainians throughout the harsh post-Soviet decades. Corruption, which external observers often view as dysfunctional, was frequently perceived locally as a mechanism to adjust to conditions under which running a business transparently was simply impossible.
1.1. The private strategy of self-protection
Whereas this shared adaptability has been central to how both societies responded to the conflict, its structural effects have diverged profoundly. In Russia, adaptability enables society to withstand the shock of the war. Economically, it allows business to operate despite harsh sanctions. Widespread expectations in 2022 of a rapid Russian economic collapse overlooked the creative strategies businesses routinely used: shell companies, intermediaries, and parallel bookkeeping.
For ordinary Russians, adaptation means low-risk self-protection: becoming invisible to the state, working informally, and securing alternative resources. More importantly, ethnographic research conducted by the Public Sociology Laboratory shows that Russians use these skills to make the war invisible to themselves. They invest significant effort in focusing on private matters, convincing themselves to patiently wait out the conflict. This attitude is often described as “fatalism.” This term is accurate only if understood as a rational strategy under constrained agency, rather than as an inherent cultural trait. Russian citizens make daily choices. If they choose to adapt, it is because it appears to be the most viable option.
When investigating Russian society today, many analysts tend to privilege structure over agency, focusing mainly on what is imposed by the authoritarian state from above, rather than on citizens’ agency. While this reflects a classic debate in social science, we need a better understanding of the everyday agency of ordinary social actors, beyond single initiatives of opposition and protest.
Adaptability also enables the Russian armed forces to innovate on the ground and to take pride in doing so. Before the war, a Russian engineer remarked to me that authorized repair centers and customer services were “for the weak.” The real skill lay in fixing high-tech licensed machinery with a screwdriver and wire. Today, this attitude persists in military production, where engineers take pride in improvising countermeasures against Ukrainian innovations.
1.2.The social logic of grassroots innovation
In this war, Russia faces a Ukrainian society where adaptation skills are even more pronounced. Decades of institutional weakness and uncertainty trained Ukrainians to operate in impossible conditions. While the media frequently uses the term “resilience” to describe Ukraine, this term is inadequate because it suggests a reality that is reactive. Instead, Ukraine displays an active “art of adaptation,” driven by a strong creative element.

Ukraine displays an active ‘art of adaptation,’ driven by a strong creative element.

The use of drones on the battlefield is abundantly documented, but its underlying social logic—a bottom-up process—is less well understood. Accounts I gather from my field observations and military analysts’ reports from the frontline reveal the grassroots level of innovation: ordinary soldiers experimenting with first-person view drones, groups of friends designing low-cost weapons or equipment. Western restrictions and delays in weapons delivery have further accelerated this grassroots innovation. Military experts contrast this adaptable “jungle” environment with the Western armed forces’ highly standardized “zoo” context.
This innovation extends deep into civil society. For instance, the widely used “Air Alert” app was built in just 72 hours following the 2022 invasion by a private IT company seeking a more efficient warning system than traditional sirens. Within three days, the developers secured a technical partner and arranged real-time data sharing with the Ministry of Defense. This ability to adapt is highly valued in Ukraine, serving as a source of pride and a core component of contemporary national identity.
Naturally, there is a darker side of adaptation, as some citizens attempt to evade military mobilization, using self-protection strategies similar to those used by Russian society, by attempting to make themselves invisible to the state. However, while draft evasion or ignoring the war is socially accepted in Russia, in Ukraine it carries a severe social cost and damages one’s social status. Understanding this divergence requires examining a second critical variable, the evolving relationship of citizens to the state.
2. Dealing with(out) the state
Distrust of the state has been a common feature of both post-Soviet societies. Before 2014, political institutions in Russia and Ukraine consistently received trust ratings below 30%, and sometimes even below 15%, according to opinion polls.
In Ukraine’s competitive political system, as well as in Russia’s increasingly authoritarian framework, public institutions were perceived as foreign bodies, potentially harmful to citizens. Since the outbreak of the conflict, this dynamic has diverged into two opposite paths: a form of loyal alienation from the state in Russia, and a critical appropriation of the state by its citizens in Ukraine.
2.1. Russia: The loyal alienation from the state
Observers often view the Russian population as either ardently pro-regime or entirely victimized by repression. This overlooks how authoritarian regimes operate, relying primarily on systematic popular demobilization. Loyal public opinion polls, as well as independent pollsters, show high approval ratings for Putin. Paradoxically, these figures confirm the depoliticization of Russian citizens: skyrocketing presidential ratings are inconsistent with the low levels of satisfaction regarding governance. There is a persistent 20-point gap between support for the president and trust in the government, parliament, or political parties. Citizens claim to trust the president but reject the institutions he controls. Innovative independent opinion polls confirm this disconnect, demonstrating that individuals intending to vote for Putin in 2024 did not expect him to implement their preferred policies.
This coexistence of loyalty and discontent is sustained by an authoritarian social contract. In exchange for stability, predictability, or resource access, citizens maintain a distance from political life, granting the regime a free hand while publicly displaying support. A striking example of this loyal alienation occurred during the partial Ukrainian occupation of the Kursk oblast. Ethnographic research conducted there by the Public Sociology Laboratory reveals that even when facing a direct threat, residents do not consider it their role to express opinions or initiate action. Respondents compared the war to a weather condition—beyond their control, requiring patience and adaptation. Perceiving the state as powerful and repressive, citizens choose not to interfere in domains deemed the exclusive prerogative of the authorities.
The authorities actively encourage this apolitical stance, remaining suspicious of any autonomous activism, whether pro- or anti-Kremlin. Military recruitment strategies reflect this, emphasizing high financial rewards and social status over patriotic mobilization. Any shift toward genuine political and open military mobilization would represent a complete breakdown of the social contract established over the last two decades.
2.2. Ukraine: The critical appropriation of the state
Conversely, the relationship of Ukrainian citizens to the state has evolved more toward an unexpected sense of civic appropriation than toward alienation. While distrust peaked during the 2013-2014 Revolution of Dignity, which rejected a corrupt state apparatus, the turning point was the subsequent threat of Russian invasion combined with the state’s evident weakness. The annexation of Crimea and the subsequent conflict in the Donbas were unequivocally interpreted as acts of external aggression against state sovereignty. Recognizing that weakened state institutions could not handle the aggression alone, ordinary citizens stepped in to fill the vacuum. While a strong state demobilized Russians, a weak state galvanized Ukrainians.

While a strong state demobilized Russians, a weak state galvanized Ukrainians.

As I have argued elsewhere, ordinary Ukrainians recognized that their weakened political institutions and armed forces could not withstand this aggression unassisted. While some external analysts anticipated a state collapse, the shock of invasion ultimately reversed this dynamic, as citizens realized public institutions could not succeed alone in defending the country.
Civilians who took up arms in 2014 frequently emphasized this distinction during interviews: “We didn’t take up arms to fight for our state, but to fight for our country.” Notwithstanding their mistrust of the political institutions, they understood that building a robust state capable of resisting external pressure required the direct, sustained investment of engaged civilians. Between 2014 and 2022, the ongoing conflict became a primary driver of bottom-up institutional reforms. Civilians stepped in wherever state structures were seen as fragile. Individuals with no prior military experience joined the armed forces; grassroots initiatives organized logistics, equipment, and medical supplies; nongovernmental organizations formed to support veterans, lobby for institutional transparency, or provide technical expertise. Importantly, this mobilization extended beyond defense: anti-corruption movements and the emergence of independent, high-quality media were direct byproducts of wartime mobilization. Countering hybrid threats also required the active coproduction of security by civil society and state actors. This temporary assumption of state functions gradually evolved into a collaborative partnership. Many volunteers and veterans joined or advised state institutions to institutionalize reforms.
By the beginning of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukrainian citizens’ relationship with the state was vastly different from 2014. Trust in the army and local authorities had risen dramatically, even as suspicion of the political class lingered. “The state has become closer to us,” confessed a young officer to me in 2023. He had been among the first civilians to head to the front line in 2014 and had remained a highly visible activist in the subsequent years. Immediately after saying that, he added: “but that doesn’t rule out certain nuances,” referring to the state’s deficiencies.

Ukraine’s institutional resilience is fundamentally anchored in its civil society, and no stable postwar settlement can be achieved without its backing.

The core of the contemporary Ukrainian civic model resides precisely within these nuances. While Ukrainian citizens today clearly support and assist public institutions, theirs is a form of critical appropriation of the state, one that involves close scrutiny of mistakes, failures, and malfunctions. As another officer emphasized in an interview: “We have to watch out and help, because we know there is always a chance the state fails.” Because Ukrainians cannot afford a state failure, this civic model is paramount for any future diplomatic or postwar considerations. Ukraine’s institutional resilience is fundamentally anchored in its civil society, and no stable postwar settlement can be achieved without its backing.
3. Deconstructed brotherhood
The third dimension concerns the evolution of mutual perceptions between Russian and Ukrainian societies. Two deeply interconnected societies are currently engaged in a war whose duration already exceeds that of the Great Patriotic War, the Soviet Union’s term of art for the Second World War. The war has profoundly transformed how Ukrainians and Russians perceive each other, a gap that deepens with every passing day. Looking back today at comparative polls on mutual perception, it is striking to see the strong sympathy between Russians and Ukrainians revealed by the results: prior to the war in 2013, around 70% of Russians and 80% of Ukrainians articulated their sympathy for the other side, though what we have observed during these 12 years of confrontation should make us very cautious about what this sympathy entails.
3.1. Russia and Ukraine through a colonial prism
During the Soviet era, the relationship between the peoples of the USSR was officially framed around the concept of “brotherhood of nations.” This brotherhood was explicitly unequal. Russia, as the “elder brother,” directed the destiny of peripheral, supposedly lesser nations. Behind the formal equality of all citizens and territories in the Soviet Union, a logic of domination and control exercised by Moscow over its peripheries operated throughout the 20th century. While early institutional designs structured the USSR as an “affirmative action empire,” later Russification policies degraded the status of local languages, cultures, and identities.
Contemporary Ukrainian discourse defines this legacy as colonial, a perspective that was long contested within Western academia. Postcolonial scholars traditionally excluded the Soviet Union from their field of study due to its nominal commitments to civic equality, formal recognition of national republics, and anti-imperialist foreign policy. Today this analytical prism is validated by the contemporary rhetoric of Russian elites, who openly deny the very existence of Ukraine. Consequently, the current war is increasingly categorized as a colonial war by Ukrainians, a vision supported by prominent scholars like Timothy Snyder.
This interpretation is reinforced by exiled national minority movements from within the Russian Federation, which express their solidarity with Ukraine, recognizing familiar patterns of identity erasure in this war that they themselves have been victims of. Inside Russia, any debate on its domination over the peripheries is nonexistent, because it is deemed dangerous for the regime’s stability. Therefore, ordinary Russians honestly struggle to understand why Ukraine actively rejects Russian language and culture, failing to see them as weapons of domination.
This framework carries profound implications for any potential resolution of the war. While political analysts sometimes claim that all armed conflicts end with an agreement and mutual concessions, one must question whether wars of decolonization follow the same logic. Is it justifiable to suggest that a colonized people meet the demands of the colonizer? Adopting a decolonial framework—in harmony with contemporary Ukrainian debates—forces us to rethink this war’s potential conclusion in entirely different terms.
3.2. The identity trap
The history of Ukraine is complex, fractured, and deeply embodied in the tragic destiny of mid-20th-century Europe. Historically, parts of modern-day Ukraine belonged to the Russian Empire. Later, eastern and central Ukraine spent 70 years under Soviet rule, whereas western Ukraine was incorporated for only half a century, following its occupation by the USSR during World War II. This nuance matters to Ukrainians. Traces and scars of border changes, repression, and violence were never erased from family memories during the Soviet years. If Ukrainians such as Slava remember the deportations of their grandparents to Siberia, it is because these memories have been passed down for generations. For Ukraine, the Second World War encapsulates both the tragedy of the Holocaust and the plight of Polish Ukrainians caught between two aggressive powers: the Soviet Union and Nazi Germany. It represents an era of impossible choices, collaboration, and deeply entrenched violence, both inflicted and endured.
This historical complexity is unacknowledged in contemporary Russia, where official historiography has legally forbidden any public discussion of instances when Russia was not on the right side of history. The Holocaust occupies a marginal place in Russian history textbooks. The events of September 1939, when the Soviet Union and Nazi Germany both invaded Poland—including parts of modern-day western Ukraine—are absent from the history of the Soviet Second World War. The Holodomor, an artificial famine imposed on Ukraine by the Soviet authorities that killed millions, is mostly unknown to Russians. Ignoring these historical blind spots makes it easier for the Russian public to project blame entirely onto the Ukrainian side.
Moving beyond the Russian regime’s manipulation of history adds even more complexity. The history of 20th-century Russia is that of a territory more isolated than we tend to think, and certainly more isolated than its former peripheries. Even though the Soviet Union carefully minimized contact between Soviet citizens and neighboring countries, border populations of the Soviet republics still retained shared histories and connections across borders—such as Kazakhs with China, Azerbaijanis with Iran, Belarusians and Ukrainians with Poland, and Moldovans with Romania.
Soviet Russia, by contrast, had far fewer external borders, especially in its heavily populated European territory, where it shared a border with only two non-Soviet neighbors: Finland and Norway. Russia’s borders were mostly with its Russified Soviet republics. As the central pivot of the Soviet system, Russia became inattentive to the historical diversity of its neighbors, minimizing the social differences between Soviet republics while emphasizing the construction of a common “Soviet nation.” The plurality of a multinational country was reduced to references to archaic folklore. The only Soviet nation allowed to have its thousand-year history taught to schoolchildren was Russia, with the other national groups’ history being considered only in relation to the Russians. Since the fall of the Soviet Union, the Russian population has struggled to understand the experiences of their former peripheries—as well as their own minorities—and to realize the extent to which its neighbors’ identities are not only post-Soviet but also linked to other cultural and political areas.

What Ukrainians are demanding from Russians today goes far beyond simply withdrawing support from the regime or condemning the war. They are asking Russians to free themselves from this imperial mindset and from any desire to interfere in their neighbors’ internal affairs.

Additionally, post-Soviet Russia struggles to define its own identity without its historical peripheries. As the historian Marlene Laruelle argues, Russia’s national self-representation is inherently imperial, referring to a territory that is larger than the state’s contemporary borders. What Ukrainians are demanding from Russians today goes far beyond simply withdrawing support from the regime or condemning the war. They are asking Russians to free themselves from this imperial mindset and from any desire to interfere in their neighbors’ internal affairs. In essence, they are calling on Russia to redefine its very identity. This is, for Ukrainians, a fundamental condition for any future reconciliation and dialogue. But it could also be a chance offered to Russian society to finally come to terms with the burden of its Soviet past.
Despite the Ukrainians’ remarkable resistance to the Russian war on meanings, the Kremlin has somehow succeeded in harming Ukrainians in their identity. The Russian framing of the current war as a denial of Ukrainian sovereignty has had a double-edged effect. On the one hand, the consistency of Ukrainian resistance today leaves no doubt about the existence of a Ukrainian nation. Ukraine has proudly earned its place on the mental map of the world, as Karl Schlögel formulated it in this same room, a place it did not have before. It is associated today with bravery, resistance, innovation, and strength. On the other hand, the focus on sovereignty imposed on Ukraine by the Russian war risks trapping the country within the narrow category of a nation-state and a rigid national identity. We see signs of that today in Ukraine in the elevated prominence of all national symbols, in references to a mythical path, and in the legitimization of all historical struggles for the Ukrainian nation, despite their dark sides. The very recent celebration of Andriy Melnyk, one of the key mid-20th-century nationalist leaders, and the naming of a military unit after a Ukrainian nationalist armed group are symptoms of this narrowing of the historical horizon.
The memory of mid-20th-century nationalist movements has been the subject of numerous debates in Ukraine since its independence. Among some, these groups were seen as fighters for the liberation of Ukraine, violently repressed by the Soviet Union because of their hostility to Moscow. However, members of these same movements perpetrated violence against Poles and Jews and collaborated with the Nazis. Many societies have complex cultures of memory. France is still struggling with the memory of the violence perpetrated by its soldiers during the Algerian War. In Ukraine, the current war makes this reckoning with the past very difficult. Contemporary Ukraine is neither rehabilitating the Nazi regime nor is it antisemitic or anti-Polish. However, the current Ukrainian resistance to Russian aggression gives renewed legitimacy to all historical struggles against Moscow, making the confrontation with Russia the core of the country’s national identity. Yet, the encouraging news is that other historical perspectives have been developed, ones centered on a global history of Ukraine. These are not limited to a narrow national framework but encompass the incredible experiences of the diverse peoples who have lived on the territory of contemporary Ukraine.
Conclusion
“I am Ukrainian.” This was the inscription on the T-shirt that Slava, the officer-turned-songwriter, wore in his most recent social media pictures. Next time we meet in Kyiv, I will probably ask him what being Ukrainian means to him. What is the space left in this identity for his Soviet childhood in the industrial Donbas? For his years of service as an elite officer in the Soviet Army, his past doubts and ignorance, his struggle for survival, his decision to embrace the destiny of Ukraine, and his sister’s choice to adopt Russia? There are no simple family histories in contemporary Russia and Ukraine. Entanglement of experiences constitutes the social fabric of both societies. Yet, I would not dare point out this complexity today to my Ukrainian friends, colleagues, and contacts. My wonderful Ukrainian colleague Olesya Khromeychuk, author of a book in which she shares the story of her brother’s loss, recounted her anger at seeing her book catalogued as “Russian literature” in a bookstore: “The only thing Russian in my book is the fact that my brother was killed by a Russian soldier.” The war has driven the two societies vastly apart, creating an abyss that will take generations to close.

Author

Anna Colin Lebedev

Senior Lecturer and Researcher, Institute of Social Sciences of Politics
- Paris Nanterre University

Assurance and Verifiability under UK SRS

What it means and what to do now

Read more

The Leeds Reforms

Financial services regulatory reforms one year on

Read more

KPMG Regulatory Barometer

Measuring the impact of regulatory and supervisory activity

Read more

Growth and competitiveness mandates and the drive for regulatory simplification continue to impact the sustainability agenda in the UK and EU.The European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) which underpin the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) have been simplified and adopted by the European Commission, to be applied for the first time for the 2027 reporting period. EFRAG has resumed its work on the sustainability reporting standard for non-EU groups (N-ESRS), with a 100-day consultation expected in the second half of July. It has also published a sustainability report based on its voluntary standard for SMEs (VSME), intended to help smaller companies to understand best practices and anticipate common hurdles in their own sustainability reporting journeys.The EBA, ESMA and EIOPA have each responded to the European Commission’s call for technical advice on reviewing the Disclosures Delegated Act (DDA) under Article 8 of the Taxonomy Regulation. All three authorities have put forward suggestions to simplify sector-specific KPIs and streamline group reporting. Final advice will be submitted to the Commission by October 2026.The UK government has endorsed the ISSB’s sustainability standards, IFRS S1 and S2, and issued the UK SRS with limited modifications. The FCA has proposed (CP26/5) to realign listed issuers’ current TCFD sustainability disclosures with the new standards, with some of the requirements on a ‘comply or explain’ basis, for accounting periods from 1 January 2027.The FCA also proposes (CP26/17) to remove the requirement for TCFD product-level reporting requirements for asset managers, life insurers and FCA-regulated pension providers from autumn 2026. Instead, institutional investors would be able to request key emissions data once a year for their own reporting requirements, and retail investors would receive relevant information about how material climate risks could affect a product’s financial performance.The UK Government committed at the end of January to moving forward with plans for a voluntary oversight regime for the assurance of sustainability-related financial disclosures, as set out in its June 2025 consultation. However, no further updates have been issued. Nor have there been any developments on the UK approach to transition plan requirements.The SFDR remains under review, with the European Commission proposing updates to make information clearer and more decision-useful for investors. Three new product categories would replace the existing Article 8 and 9 classifications: transition products (Article 7), ESG basics (Article 8) and sustainable features (Article 9). Each category would have a 70% investment threshold to be held in line with a binding investment strategy – to note, this is inconsistent with ESMA’s fund name guidelines, which require a threshold of 80% for certain fund names. The European Parliament and European Council have set out their draft positions but, with trilogue negotiations still to come, the final SFDR text is unlikely to be agreed by the end of 2026.In May, ESMA also urged national competent authorities (NCAs) to take a more proportionate approach to supervising sustainability requirements.The impacts of climate and nature-related risk on financial stability are front of mind for prudential regulators. The June 2026 deadline has passed for UK firms to develop ‘credible and ambitious’ plans for the management of climate-related financial risk, as set out in PRA PS25/25 and SS5/25. With the initial six-month period now concluded, we may see supervisors starting to ask firms for evidence of their internal reviews and action plans.Meanwhile, the ECB published two ‘good practice’ reports in May, one on overall climate and nature (C&N) risk management and the other on C&N stress testing. Most of the newly added good practices in the first report related to nature risks, prudential transition planning, physical risks and the management of reputational and litigation risks. The second report found that all significant institutions had integrated climate risk into their stress-testing frameworks, but that there was still room for improvement, particularly in integrating C&N risks into modelling approaches.In June, the EBA published the draft methodology, templates and guidance for its 2027 EU-wide stress test, which will integrate climate risks for the first time through a dedicated module. At the start of 2026 it also consulted on updating the systemic risk buffer guidelines to include climate-related exposures – the amended guidelines are yet to be issued.EIOPA is consulting on the prudential treatment of adaptation measures under the Solvency II framework, with policy output expected in Q4 2026. It also published a discussion paper with the European Stability Mechanism (ESM), outlining a European risk-sharing mechanism, based on a natural catastrophe insurance pool and a loan-based backstop, to manage the financial fallout from large natural catastrophes. To note, this paper does not constitute formal regulatory proposals at this stage.The EU ESG ratings regime went live on 2 July, with ESMA supervising methodology transparency, governance and conflicts of interest. Most ratings providers must apply for authorisation by 2 November 2026. Third parties, including fund managers, may continue to distribute ratings while applications, registrations or notifications are pending. After that date, they will only be able to distribute ratings from providers listed on ESMA’s Article 14 register.ESMA has also consulted on guidelines on the endorsement mechanism for ESG ratings issued by third-country ratings providers. The consultation proposed requirements on expertise, accountability, governance, periodic reviews, information-sharing within the group and likely information requests from ESMA, with final guidelines to apply from 2 August 2026.The FCA has consulted on a UK regime for ESG ratings providers, with requirements largely the same as the EU. It has proposed a 12-month application window beginning in June 2027, with the regime to go live in June 2028. Firms should note some of the nuanced differences between the two regimes, for example on scope and exclusions, mitigating versus managing conflicts of interest, and prescriptive versus principles-based governance requirements.Meanwhlie, the European Commission has updated the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) benchmark values for the period 2026–2030 to ensure they remain current and support decarbonisation efforts while maintaining competitiveness. A comprehensive review of the EU ETS is due to take place in July 2026 and will introduce sector-specific fallback benchmarks.Finally, the FCA has shared examples of good and poor practice in relation to the UK Sustainability Disclosure Requirements. It has also considered barriers to scaling finance for climate solutions and highlighted challenges in attracting private capital and matching capital properly to opportunities, and frictions caused by information and capacity gaps.

At a glance – watch out for:H2 2026 – EBA revised systemic risk buffer guidance (originally expected mid-2026)July 2026 – EFRAG consultation on N-ESRSJuly 2026 – European Commission review of the EU ETS2 August 2026 – application of ESMA guidelines on ESG ratings third-country endorsement mechanism2 November 2026 – deadline for ESG ratings authorisation applications/notifications to ESMAOctober 2026 – final Taxonomy reporting technical advice from EBA, ESMA and EIOPA to the European CommissionAutumn 2026 – implementation of streamlined FCA TCFD product-disclosuresQ4 2026 – UK SRS disclosures for listed companies FCA policy statementQ4 2026 – FCA policy statement on regulating ESG rating providersQ4 2026 – EIOPA policy on prudential treatment of adaptation measures2027 – reporting periods from when revised ESRS will become mandatory and UK SRS disclosures are expected to apply to listed companiesMarch 2027 – Deadline to transpose the revised CSRD into national lawJune 2027 – application window opens for ESG ratings providers in the UKJune 2028 – UK ESG ratings regime go-live

articles.title: Daily: Add quality bonds as yields should fall
articles.text:
Talk to a UBS Financial AdvisorFrom the studioVideo: Top of Mind in APAC | The current bull market and risks to watch (5 mins)Video: Market Playbook | Why investors should revisit Europe (4 mins)Video: The Deep Dive | Upgrading India (6 mins)Thought of the dayUS Treasury yields are approaching their recent highs in May as escalating hostilities in the Middle East and rising energy prices have rekindled inflation fears and concerns that the Federal Reserve may need to raise policy rates in the near term. The 10-year Treasury yield stood at 4.66% at the time of writing, just shy of the May peak of 4.68%.The Iran-aligned Houthis attacked two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea as part of a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, disrupting another vital waterway for global energy supplies. The US continues its strikes to “further degrade” Iran’s ability to threaten ship traffic, while Iran’s Revolutionary Guards warned that no tanker would be allowed to enter or leave the Strait of Hormuz without coordination with the Islamic Republic. Brent crude oil was trading above USD 97/bbl at the time of writing, having risen by over 33% since the start of this month.But we continue to see scope for yields to drift lower over the coming quarters, and believe quality fixed income offers an attractive combination of income, diversification, and medium-term return potential.Energy disruptions from the Middle East should ease over time. Investors should be prepared for further hostilities, with regional mediators’ ongoing attempts to bring the US and Iran back to the negotiating table so far proving unsuccessful. But US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the US remains open to a diplomatic solution, and Trump this week claimed that oil prices will go down, saying “just give me a little time.” Our view remains that the US and Iran will eventually seek a path toward a diplomatic framework as economic pressures mount, and that oil prices could return to levels that would keep inflation under control.Price pressure should continue to moderate. Despite the flare-up in geopolitical tensions, inflation expectations remain lower than their recent peaks. The 10-year breakeven inflation rate stood at around 2.25%, compared with 2.5% in May. The consumer survey by the University of Michigan in July also showed a decline in year-ahead inflation expectations, with five-year expectations holding steady at the lowest level since March. Separately, the June consumer price index showed that monthly underlying inflation, which excludes volatile items like energy and food, fell for the first time since 2020. This supports our view that Fed policy is already sufficiently restrictive and that inflation should continue to trend lower without the need for a meaningful further increase in rates.The next Fed move remains more likely to be a cut. Elevated AI infrastructure investment and the associated rise in asset prices have dominated US economic activity, with households on aggregate experiencing flat or negative real wage growth. With the personal savings rate nearing a historical low, and the labor market showing little evidence of tightening, we expect softer growth conditions to emerge in the coming months as fiscal support moderates. In our view, a more modest inflation environment, combined with potentially softer labor demand over time due to increasing AI adoption, should push the Fed to a less hawkish stance and a resumption of gradually easing policy rates to around the 3% neutral estimate.So, we anticipate Treasury yields will fall over the remainder of the year, generating potential capital gains alongside attractive carry for bondholders. We think the two- to five-year segment offers the most favorable risk-reward profile. For a holistic and well-diversified fixed income allocation, we favor select exposure to higher-yielding bond market segments such as emerging markets or high yield, equity income strategies, and yield-generating structured strategies.

articles.title: Uniswap: DeFi's fee machine behind Robinhood Chain
articles.text: Uniswap, the fee machine at the heart of Robinhood's new chain4 min readWhen Robinhood switched on the public mainnet of Robinhood Chain on 1 July, most of the attention went to the headline products: tokenised stocks tradable around the clock in more than 120 countries, perpetual futures in the wallet, agentic trading accounts.1 The more revealing detail sat lower in the announcement. Among the chain's day-one partners, the brokerage with 27.7 million funded customers named Uniswap, which is deploying a dedicated AMM to serve as a primary public liquidity protocol.1It is worth asking why a company of Robinhood's scale leans on existing DeFi infrastructure for the most critical piece of its exchange stack. The fee data explains why that choice carried so little risk.The largest fee generator in DeFi historyUniswap has now collected over $5.0B in cumulative trading fees, more than any other decentralised protocol ever built.2Cumulative fees, all crypto applications, as of 15 July 20262Only the stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle have earned more, and both are centralised companies running money-market operations. Strip those out and Uniswap sits alone at the top of decentralised protocols.2The run rate remains substantial. Over the past 30 days, Uniswap generated $42.8M in fees on $38.3B of spot volume, an annualised pace of roughly $520M.2 To put that in perspective, users have paid more to trade on Uniswap’s deployment on Robinhood Chain in 15 days since launch ($13.2M) than they have paid in base-layer fees on Ethereum ($8.2M), Bitcoin ($5.8M), Solana ($13.8M) and Base ($2.3M) over the past 30 days.2 An application is out-earning the blockchains it runs on.The caveat: activity is well off its cycle peak. Monthly fees topped $115.9M in October 2025 and have since settled into a $34M to $49M range through 2026.2 Fee income at Uniswap is a function of volatility and volume, and both have cooled. The application durability balances the picture. Live since 2018, Uniswap has generated fees without interruption through two full market cycles, across four protocol versions, on multiple chains, without custody, order books or market-making agreements. A brokerage integrating an exchange needs exactly that property: liquidity infrastructure that keeps functioning whether markets are euphoric or dead. Years of uninterrupted fee generation are the closest thing DeFi has to an operating track record.The fee switch changes the storyWhat has changed is who gets paid. For most of its existence, Uniswap passed every dollar of fees to liquidity providers while the protocol, and UNI holders, earned nothing. That ended on 27 December 2025, when the long-debated fee switch went live. The protocol now retains roughly 9.5% of total fees, about $4.1M over the past 30 days, with the remaining 90.5% still flowing to LPs.2 At the current pace that is close to $50M of annualised protocol revenue, modest against a $5B fee history, but it converts Uniswap from a public utility into something an investor can actually value.That makes the Robinhood integration more than a distribution win. Tokenised stocks swapped through Uniswap's AMM on Robinhood Chain generate the same swap fees that built those numbers. Could tokenised equities become Uniswap's next fee leg? In its first week, Robinhood Chain recorded roughly $570M of DEX volume on about $22M of liquidity, much of it memecoin speculation rather than stock tokens.3 Against $38B of monthly Uniswap spot volume that is a rounding error, but it is a new asset class, attached to a retail funnel of 27.7 million customers, on a chain where Uniswap is a flagship venue.Fee generation has always been the cleanest measure of product-market fit in crypto. On that measure, Robinhood didn't take a risk. It picked the incumbent.SourcesRobinhood Markets, "Robinhood Accelerates Global Expansion with Robinhood Chain Mainnet, Stock Tokens, Agentic Trading and New Suite of DeFi Products", 1 July 2026Token Terminal, data as of 15 July 2026crypto.news, "Robinhood Chain did $570m volume on $21m of liquidity: the launch week autopsy", July 2026Published onJul 24th, 2026WriterJérémy Le BescontLead Content ManagerFormer journalist for Le Monde, Le Figaro, and Capital's Cryptocurrency section. Bitcoin node runner.

articles.text:
Protecting our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity

Protecting Our Clients Against Potentially Fraudulent Activity
Across the industry, we are seeing an increase in bad actors impersonating and misusing corporate brands to get access to personal information and funds from unsuspecting individuals. These activities may involve individuals acting as company representatives and may include fake websites, social media inquiries, or communications that closely resemble official channels.
Please read the below for important reminders that can help protect you from potentially fraudulent activity.
We strongly caution against providing personal data or transferring funds in response to unsolicited requests. For your safety, always verify the authenticity of communications claiming to be from Lazard by contacting us through our official website or known contact points.
Specifically, Lazard will never engage in the following activities:

Sending unsolicited investment proposals or requests for personal information from nonverified persons.
Requesting payments to bank accounts in the names of individuals, third parties, unknown company names, or through payment intermediaries.
Offering unrealistically attractive returns that seem too good to be true.
Expressing urgency to complete an investment or make a payment.
Requesting additional payments to release investments that have already been made.
Requesting money to be sent via social media messaging apps and/or platforms.

If you believe that you have fallen victim to fraud, please contact your bank immediately. Additionally, you should report the incident to law enforcement in your jurisdiction as soon as possible.
The safety and protection of data and information is a priority for Lazard, and we appreciate your careful attention and diligence.
***
Lazard cannot accept any responsibility for any loss, damage, or claims arising from fraudulent activities. Please fully read account disclosures and related policies.

articles.title: Hedge Fund Outlook H2 2026
articles.text:
Investment Outlook

Hedge Funds

Alternative Assets

Diversification

Artificial Intelligence

Real Assets

23 July, 2026

25 minutes

Hedge Fund Outlook H2 2026

EDM
Asset Class ViewsEN

Hedge Fund Outlook H2 2026

25 minutes

EDM
Asset Class ViewsEN

Summary

Introduction

Hedge fund (HF) performance remained strong in H1 2026. Industry alpha also stayed elevated. The quality of HF returns, combined with investors’ search for diversification and the headline noise surrounding private assets, has continued to attract flows into the industry. H2 2026 should remain supportive for HF. But this is not a regime of abundant, easy beta. It is a narrower, more selective, capex-driven market, where support exists but does not diffuse evenly across the economy or across assets. Markets are moving from broad exposure to selection, from owning the headline theme to discriminating within it. For HF, H2 will likely be less about calling the market than about identifying the right structural themes, separating true winners from those merely riding the theme, and getting the timing right in a market prone to faster rotations. That is the kind of environment in which HF can do well.

8 macro themes that will matter for HF

The cycle remains strong enough to preserve risk appetite, but not strong enough to lift everything indiscriminately. It is also not weak enough to trigger a full defensive regime. This kind of backdrop typically favours fundamental pricing, sector rotation and alpha, rather than blind beta. It also tends to generate more frequent asset rotations.For HF, this implies that broad market exposure should do less of the work than in H1, while stock, sector and country selection should do more. That is constructive for L/S equity, Event-Driven strategies and selective EM specialists. The main risk is that macro headlines can still periodically distort the tape and create violent but short-lived anomalies.

In H2, the marginal dollar of growth should still be directed toward AI, power, grids, energy security, defence, strategic autonomy and supply-chain reshaping. In short, the marginal dollar relates to building, not buying. That matters because capex-led growth tends to be narrower, more policy-shaped, more sector-concentrated and less broadly diffused through the economy than during a consumption-led cycle. This has two consequences. First, segments outside that epicentre can run on their own tape, which supports dispersion. Second, differentiation should rise within the epicentre itself. AI is the clearest example. After months of focusing on a handful of obvious winners, markets are now debating who will actually capture the value inside the chain (see the convergence across AI segments, shown below for the US).That is very supportive for directional L/S equity, thematic specialists, Event-Driven strategies and selective L/S credit. The risks are equally clear: crowded longs, violent rotations within the same structural complex, and portfolios that appear diversified while all leaning on the same capex regime.

Monetary policies are diverging, but not enough to create dominant macro trades. Most central banks are close to equilibrium, within one cut/hike of cu rent pricing. Where neutrality lies, how much term premium belongs in the curves, who owns duration and how investors are positioned should matter more than the level of rates alone. Dispersion will come from different mixes of inflation stickiness, growth resilience, fiscal and debt pressure, central banks’ forward guidance and tolerance for inflation staying away from target. So, the debate is moving away from purely cyclical drivers of yields toward more structural ones. Large directional trades may be scarcer, but monetary divergence should still generate many local relative opportunities across rates, inflation curves, cross-market bond instruments and FX.

Liquidity remains available, but it is less generous than headline market conditions suggest. Market liquidity overstates true macro liquidity – which is closer to neutral in our view. Plumbing remains under persistent stress. While a major liquidity accident is not our base case, the backdrop should lead to faster asset rotations. The market beta contribution can remain positive, but more fragile liquidity can generate an adverse asymmetry of risk (a convexity risk).Credit markets are moving into a more mature mid-cycle phase. Funding remains open, but tolerance for weak balance sheets, poor cash conversion, high refinancing needs and long-duration promises is eroding. That is a healthy shift for hedge funds: it improves alpha conditions by forcing more fundamental discrimination and by creating more tactical trading windows.This should favour fundamental L/S strategies in both equity and credit, as well as lower-net strategies. More broadly, the combination of positive but fragile beta, faster rotation risk and sharper leverage unwind dynamics creates an asymmetric risk profile which makes HF increasingly attractive relative to fully invested styles.

The old divide between rich and poor households, shareholders and workers was largely shaped by globalisation, deindustrialisation and increasingly shareholder-centric capitalism. That logic is now broadening. AI, geopolitical fragmentation, energy and sovereign security, protectionism and reindustrialisation are widening the gap between winners and losers at every level of the economy.The K-shape is no longer just a household or labour story. It is becoming a system-wide sorting mechanism, creating new winners and losers across countries, sectors, business models and corporate balance sheets. The K-shape is going micro.This is increasingly visible in the market structure, through low pairwise correlations, elevated dispersion and narrower breadth. That is fertile ground for stock picking and pair trades. The main risks are herding on the long side and falling into value traps, because some securities may remain cheap for good reason while early winners are not always the final winners. Those risks are already visible in themes such as AI and defence.

Geopolitics will remain a key variable, but H2 may bring less chaos. Middle East tensions may stay heated, but be less market-dominating. Ukraine remains u resolved, but is less likely to drive the daily tape. US trade policy may stay restrictive, but become less erratic. The European regulatory tone may turn somewhat more supportive of strategic consolidation. Lower policy volatility and fewer abrupt shifts in regulation or tax policy could be enough to support M&A, carve outs, asset sales, activism, liability management, buybacks and strategic reviews.

This is an obvious positive for Event-Driven and L/S equity with catalyst. More importantly, the quality of the opportunity set should improve, with a richer pipeline of complex, more attractive situations. The main downside is that more corporate activity also increases the risk of short squeezes for L/S equity.

AI, power, energy security, defence and strategic autonomy are different faces of the same structural complex. Many portfolios might therefore be less diversified than they appear. The next unwind might be less about crowding than about hidden sameness in portfolios. Rising correlation across momentum drivers makes this risk even more relevant. Concentration and higher trading leverage also increase the risk of co-movement. In that context, the search for more robust diversification should continue to support HF, thanks to their arbitrage approach, lower net exposure and the complementary contribution from cash.

Broad passive and static factor frameworks might increasingly miss where the real action is. Markets are now shaped by secular capex, policy distortions, narrow leadership, unstable correlations and polarised earnings outcomes. Factor investing still matters, but it works in a less linear and less reliable way than before. Broad factors will likely be less efficient at capturing internal fragmentation and shifting thematic leadership. That should favour discretionary stockpickers, adaptive quant, thematic specialists, catalystdriven equity and active relative value over static factorneutral books and passive allocators.

Special focus: HF exposure to and risk from AI

Our analysis shows that HF exposure to AI, a theme likely to remain central in H2, is heterogeneous in size, implementation and risk. This analysis is based on in-house AI thematic baskets and HF sensitivity models. Directional L/S equity shows the clearest exposure. Since 2025, AI has risen to roughly one-fifth of total beta and has accounted for about one-third of YTD performance. Exposure is concentrated primarily in the US, with selective EU exposure and, more recently, Japan and China AI-related names. It is also dynamic rather than static and, until recently, tilted more toward mid- and downstream segments.

L/S Equity Neutral show limited AI beta as expected, expressing the theme through relative positions. The contribution has been material and likely negative YTD due to frequent AI rotations. L/S credit focuses on funding the build-out through HY and ABS, while shorting business models disrupted by AI. The YTD contribution from the theme has been broadly neutral. Global macro’s AI exposure remains mostly indirect, via rates, FX, energy and Asian supply chains.Put differently: directional L/S equity owns AI, L/S neutral arbitrages it, L/S credit funds it, and macro feels it through spillovers.

The key AI message for H2 is that the easy money is behind us, but not the story. The ecosystem is moving from buildout euphoria to monetisation scrutiny, and is fra menting into clearer winners and losers. Funding conditions still suggest capital remains available. But bottom-up fundamentals increasingly point to rising capex burdens, lagging monetisation proof and leverage metrics are becoming less comfortable for some of the biggest spenders. The greatest strain sits with the capex anchors (hyperscalers and other major spenders). Other parts of the chain, such as infrastructure suppliers, data centres and more visible monetisers, still look healthier. Utilities and power remain acceptable, but their outlook depends heavily on timing, funding costs and regulation. For HF, the AI arbitrage is therefore not simply about rotating into “safe” enablers, because monetisation pressure is likely to travel through the chain. If pressure rises on the major spenders, they may respond by repricing access, tightening terms, slowing spend or squeezing suppliers. The true distinction is not between AI spenders and “risk-free” enablers, but between those with pricing power and bottlenecks, and those forced to absorb the capital burden. For HF, the key question is no longer whether AI can be financed, but where the cost of that financing will ultimately be borne across the ecosystem.From another perspective, HF are also increasingly users of AI in their own investment processes. The most sophisticated ones are deploying language models and machine learning to improve signal generation, portfolio construction and risk management. Managers with advanced AI tools may gain an edge.

HF strategy review for H2 2026

L/S Equity: themes are consensus; picking winners and losers is not Directional L/S equity tends to work best when beta contribution is fading, stock dispersion is healthy, correlations are low enough to let selection matter, and fundamentals and catalysts still shape the tape. H2 looks close to that sweet spot. Capexled growth is narrow and differentiated, corporate activity is reviving, the opportunity set remains supportive, and broad beta has already done much of the work YTD. The cleanest hunting grounds are the US, Japan and selective EM. Europe and the UK appear more average, as rates and top-down noise continue to distort the tape more heavily.The key point is that the main inefficiency is not in spotting the right themes – they are already well known – but in ranking who captures the value within them. That calls for deeper fundamental work, not simply thematic ownership. The main risk is the higher probability of faster and more frequent rotations, driven by leverage, occasional rate shocks or geopolitics interrupting stock-specific narratives.

The bar is somewhat higher for L/S equity neutral. That strategy works best when micro dispersion comes with stable relative relationships, a usable factor structure and enough internal logic for mean reversion or sector RV to matter. H2 offers the dispersion, but only part of the stability. The factor map is less reliable because sector and thematic narratives dominate, micro rotations are becoming more frequent, while funds focus on momentum. Neutrality therefore becomes harder to achieve in practice. On the positive side, the K-shape dispersion means the short book is as important as the long book – with structurally impaired business models, AI-disrupted incumbents and capex-heavy balance sheets offering increasingly compelling short candidates. All in all, sector specialists, adaptive quant managers and fundamentally driven neutral styles should still do well, while static factor-neutral books and broad style arbitrage look riskier.

Merger Arbitrage: the pipeline is back – and becoming more interestingFinancing remains available, boards are becoming more willing to act, and the strategic need for industrial reshuffling is rising. The real improvement is not only in deal volume, but in the composition of the pipeline. Plain-vanilla deals still provide carry, but H2 should also bring more complex, more strategic, more hostile and more sponsor-involved situations, with richer event paths around votes, approvals and financing. A higher share of non-pure-cash deals also supports the opportunity set by creating more nuanced spread profiles. Regulation remains manageable in enough jurisdictions to keep the strategy attractive. In Europe, strategic consolidation and “national champion” logic may create a somewhat friendlier backdrop, although antitrust and crossborder sensitivities have not disappeared. In the US, the environment should remain case-by-case: less uniformly hostile than at the peak of regulatory activism, but it is still strict in strategic sectors and in transactions with national-security implications. Merger arbitrage does not require a calm market. It requires usable confidence, i.e. enough visibility regarding financing, regulation and strategic rationale over a 6 to-12-month horizon. Deal spreads have become more attractive partly because the market is demanding a healthier complexity risk premium. Added to that, synthetic cash still matters in a world of positive real yields. Overall, the strategy should do well in H2.

L/S Credit: right phase, but dislocations are not there yetL/S Credit is entering a favourable phase conceptually: a mid-cycle in which financing remains open, with markets becoming more discriminating towards weak balance sheets, poor cash conversion, refinancing pressure, long-duration stories and situations where equity enthusiasm outruns credit quality.However, ample perceived market liquidity is preventing clear differentiation just yet. Credit dispersion remains insufficient to implement juicy enough long and short positions, while spreads are tight and not dislocated enough. In other words, the backdrop is constructive on paper, but still selective in reality. A shock or valuation reset would be welcome to restore the opportunity set.

EM Fixed-Income/Macro: rich in diversity but still hostage to AI and US ratesThe EM macro backdrop remains supportive enough. Structural vulnerability is manageable in aggregate and has improved, lowering tail risk and allowing investors to access the asset class more comfortably. Liquidity conditions remain uneven, but have loosened overall. Inflation is easing, rates can stabilise or move lower, and risk adjusted carry remains attractive. In that sense, beta exposure still looks appealing.There are multiple fault lines in EM markets (the “EM” label itself is becoming less and less relevant) running across AI-linked Asia, China-exposure, oil sensitivity, reformers versus fragile financers. Yet, differentiation is still only partly expressed because EM markets are still too dependent on tech/AI and US rates. Correlations across EM credit segments remain elevated and credit dislocations are still limited. That is why we expect more local relative trades across rates, FX and credit than a few blockbuster trades. EM-focused HF should continue to provide access to the space with an enhanced risk/reward profile.

Global Macro: less about the cycle, more about its fracturesOn balance, the environment is positive for Global Macro. We don’t see the major economic dislocations that usually create the most attractive opportunities. But the K shape should continue to feed divergences in growth, inflation, monetary policy and fiscal stress. At the same time, markets should become more fundamentally driven, liquidity more discriminating, and the macro scenario somewhat clearer – all of which tend to support risk-taking and more tactical opportunities.

Thus, we expect a diversity of smaller relative trades and market-timing opportunities, rather than a few dominant directional trades. Structural inflation, monetary neutrality, sovereign bond ownership and positioning, fiscal constraints and FX credibility will be central themes. Those themes are likely to be expressed through sophisticated relative trades across rates, inflation curves, bond instruments, selective FX and commodities – where energy, power and grid investments intersect with structural inflation and supply dynamics. In other words, Global Macro in H2 will be less about calling cyclical levels than about arbitraging fragmentation and the forces shaping markets beneath the surface: ownership structure, positioning, flows and premium repricing, which can move markets without a decisive fundamental catalyst.

CTAs: trends are there, favouring nimble over patientThe aggregate directional pulse remains favourable, fewer assets are trapped in range trading, and our model of trendfollowing potential remains decent. Cross-asset correlations have also receded, giving CTAs more room to raise risk budgets. However, as the market moves into a different phase from H1, trends will likely need to refresh. Some existing positions are maturing, while others are constrained by a range-bound dollar and relatively tight rate differentials. There is a logic to asset trendiness. Strong trendiness in equities usually comes with weaker trendiness in bonds, and vice versa – because equities are most directional when the discount-rate backdrop is stable, whereas bond trends become strongest when inflation and central-bank repricing take over as the main market driver. Trendiness in bonds often leads to trends in FX via changing rate differentials, provided regional divergence is strong enough. Commodity trends can trigger opportunities in bonds, but only when they materially affect inflation. Equity trends dominated H1; H2 may see more opportunities in bonds and commodities, and later in FX. We expect more short- to medium-term trend opportunities in H2 than a long-lasting trend regime. That argues for a broadly neutral stance. Timing CTAs is always difficult, which also argues for maintaining a core allocation.

Conclusion

For H2 2026, we expect a narrower beta market and a broader alpha market. The opportunity set should be healthier at the micro level, while top-down strategies should find many local relative trends rather than major directional trades. This is not a market in which hedge funds win because markets are broken, but because markets are becoming more selective and shifting. Our preference remains for directional L/S equity and merger arbitrage, but the backdrop is not polarised enough to justify a narrow strategy call. A combination of bottom-up and top-down strategies looks best suited to H2.

Authors

Jean-Baptiste BERTHON

Senior Cross-Asset Strategist, Amundi Investment Institute

Alexandre Lefebvre

Global Head of Real & Alternative Assets, Amundi

articles.title: The Hidden Costs of Downtime 2026
articles.text:
Consulting Report

22 Jul 2026

The Hidden Costs of Downtime 2026

A $600 billion wake-up call, in partnership with Splunk

Oxford Economics and Splunk captured responses from 2,000 executives from Global 2000 companies to analyse the immediate and long-term effects of downtime triggered by cybersecurity incidents.

Downtime has stopped being just an IT headache and become a boardroom crisis. As organisations lean further into interconnected digital ecosystems — third-party vendors, cloud providers, and now autonomous AI agents — every new link becomes another point of failure, and the fallout from a single outage spreads faster and farther than ever. Splunk’s research with Oxford Economics reveals the scale of that spread: outages now ripple into regulatory fines, ransomware payouts, stock price dips, and reputational damage.

This report invites the reader to uncover where outages actually originate, from everyday human error to sophisticated cyberattacks, and why the toll is proving harder to contain. You’ll see how AI is reshaping the equation, helping teams resolve incidents faster while introducing new failure modes of its own. Readers will also find strategies resilient organisations are using to treat downtime as a business risk and build the kind of predictive immunity that separates market leaders from the rest.

Shifting Gears: Construction’s New Growth Drivers

in this page:

Australia’s construction sector is shifting gears. Data centres and non-residential investment are stepping up as engines of growth while engineering firms pivot from transport megaprojects toward the infrastructure of the energy transition. Beneath these shifts, the sector continues to grapple with capacity constraints, elevated costs and a tight labour market that will shape how far and how fast activity can grow.

This conference brings together Oxford Economics’ construction and macro specialists to unpack these shifting growth engines and what they mean for capacity, costs and strategy over the decade ahead.

articles.title: Gavekal Technologies: New Energy
articles.text:
Gavekal Technologies: New Energy

Most recent

Gavekal Technologies: New Energy

EVs’ Year Of Living Dangerously

AJ Cortese, Ernan Cui
21 Jul 2026

China’s passenger car market is having a terrible 2026, and electric vehicles for once are no exception. Prices and margins are under pressure. Yet despite all that, the market is not consolidating—quite the opposite. What makes it all possible is exports, which now account for a third of Chinese EV makers’ unit sales. The question is how long international markets will be willing to absorb the rising tide of Chinese imports.

Gavekal Technologies: Briefing

Five Questions On China Biotech

Tom Hancock, AJ Cortese, Huang Shichan
13 Jul 2026

Investors have cooled on China’s biotechnology sector, after a spectacular run-up in Hong Kong biotech stocks in early 2025. This is a needed correction: China’s biotech companies are technologically strong, but commercially immature. Also in today’s China Tech Brief: drones and EVs.

More research

The New Energy System Takes Shape

6 Jul 2026

China’s latest five-year plan for energy disappointed many analysts because of its unambitious targets for scaling back fossil fuel use. This misses the point. The plan is important because for the first time, Beijing is formally committing to an energy system based mainly on non-fossil fuels, with traditional coal, oil and gas as backup stabilizers. Achieving this goal will take another couple of decades, but policymakers are already starting to look beyond brute additions of renewables capacity to the efficiency measures that will be required for success.

Tesla’s Two Way Bet In Physical AI

29 Jun 2026

Tesla’s market capitalization is by far the biggest among global automakers, mainly because it has sold itself as a leader in AI—not just in cars, but for humanoid robots as well. To turn its AI vision into reality, it needs China. Its Shanghai gigafactory enabled Tesla to scale up electric vehicle production; to scale up robotaxis and humanoids, it will have to figure out how to operate in both the US and China even as the two countries wall off their AI ecosystems from each other.

How The US Can Meet AI Energy Demand

22 Jun 2026

Conventional wisdom has held that while China’s AI buildout is constrained by lack of access to advanced chips, the US will be slowed by the scarcity and cost of electricity. Solving the power constraint is indeed a problem: AI data centers are suddenly adding a lot of new electricity
demand on a system that has not grown in two decades. But aside from building new power plants and transmission lines—a long slog—there is a lot the US can do to squeeze more juice out of the current infrastructure.

The China Shock Comes For Asia

15 Jun 2026

Europe fears that subsidized and efficient Chinese high-tech companies will de-industrialize the continent. But the “second China shock” is arguably even more of a threat to northeast Asia, where China’s lead in batteries, electric vehicles and solar has Tokyo and Seoul incumbents worried that machine tools, robots and displays could be next. But Japan and South Korea should be able to hang on to large and profitable chunks of their industrial bases, thanks to both technological factors and geopolitics.

China’s Nuclear Spring

8 Jun 2026

Nuclear power is back in business, thanks to the AI datacenter boom and renewed worries about fossil-fuel security following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Despite brave talk in the US, China is at the forefront of that revival and will remain so for another decade.

China’s Export-Control Calculus

1 Jun 2026

As Washington discovered with semiconductors, export controls that aim to maintain a technological lead are double-edged. They may slow a rival’s catch-up, but they also incentivize the rival’s innovation and harm domestic interests. And they are hard to enforce. China is rapidly expanding its export controls to include not just rare earths but many other technologies where it has a lead. But the more controls it imposes, the more it risks choking off revenues and paths to innovation for its leading tech companies.
